passage: I'm Payal, and Francis lives in the flat next to mine in Berlin. He moved from Kochi two years ago for an engineering job. In the first winter I heard him on the phone to his mother, speaking Malayalam, sounding homesick. He barely left his flat. Then I saw him at the German classes in the community centre, sitting in the front row. By spring he was cooking fish curry for our building's summer party. People lined up for seconds. He also joined a local cycling club. Last month he told me he still goes to the Kerala association once a month for Onam and songs. He said, 'I don't have to choose.' He seemed lighter saying it.

qa.q: Which city did Francis move from?
qa.a: He moved from Kochi.

qa.q: What does Francis barely leaving his flat in the first winter suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt lonely and homesick, missing his family and home.

qa.q: What helped Francis build belonging in Berlin?
qa.a: Learning German, sharing his food, joining a cycling club and keeping ties with the Kerala association.

qa.q: How does Payal see Francis's change over time?
qa.a: Payal sees him moving from lonely to settled, keeping his roots while making new connections.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young migrant adapt to a new country while keeping his identity.

passage:
First week: Kishore moved from Patna to Chennai for work. He couldn't read the Tamil signs, and the food felt strange. He ate instant noodles in his room and called home every night.

Second month: His colleague Gurpreet, who'd moved from Amritsar a year before, took him to a small mess run by a Bihari family. Kishore nearly cried eating litti chokha. Gurpreet also dragged him to a Tamil class on Saturdays. "You'll feel less like a guest," she said.

Sixth month: Kishore could order at the tea shop in Tamil, to the owner's delight. He'd started liking filter coffee. He still missed Chhath at home, but that year he celebrated it by the Marina beach with other migrants.

qa.q: What did Kishore eat in his room in the first week?
qa.a: He ate instant noodles.

qa.q: Why did Kishore nearly cry eating litti chokha?
qa.a: The familiar food from home touched his homesickness and made him feel comforted.

qa.q: What helped Kishore feel less like a guest?
qa.a: Learning Tamil, finding familiar food and friends, and joining other migrants for Chhath.

qa.q: How might the tea shop owner see Kishore's effort to speak Tamil?
qa.a: The owner was delighted, probably feeling respected by his effort to learn the local language.

grounding: Shows a young man over months adapting to a new city while keeping his home traditions.

passage: Mohit beta, you're leaving for Canada next month, so let me, your Rekha-bua, tell you something. I went to London at twenty-three as a nurse. The first year, I hid my accent and never brought dal to work because someone once wrinkled their nose. I felt like half a person. Then an older Jamaican nurse told me, "Bring your food. We'll trade." She taught me her patties, I taught her rajma. Slowly I stopped hiding. I made English friends, joined the choir at the hospital, but kept my Sunday phone calls home and my Diwali lamps. You don't have to become someone else to belong. Take what's good there, and keep what's good in you.

qa.q: What did Rekha teach the Jamaican nurse to cook?
qa.a: She taught her rajma.

qa.q: What did Rekha mean by feeling 'like half a person'?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and incomplete, hiding parts of herself like her accent and her dal, so she didn't feel whole.

qa.q: What advice does Rekha give Mohit before he leaves?
qa.a: Take what's good in the new country and keep what's good in himself, without becoming someone else.

qa.q: How might the Jamaican nurse have seen Rekha's food?
qa.a: She saw it as something to share and trade, not something strange.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on how she adapted abroad while preserving identity and building belonging.

passage:
Dhruv's first Diwali in Rotterdam came with sideways rain and a cancelled tram.
He had planned it carefully: diyas bought from an Indian grocery two towns away, his mother's besan laddoo recipe on a voice note, and an invitation to Manoj's flat. Manoj was the only other Indian on his team and had lived there four years.
Now he stood under a bus shelter with a box of half-set laddoos going soft in the damp. For a moment he missed Jaipur so sharply it felt like hunger: the noise, the rooftops, his cousins lighting sparklers too close to the curtains.
He almost went home. Instead he texted Manoj, "Running late, still coming," and walked the whole way.
At the flat were Manoj, two Dutch colleagues and a Brazilian neighbour, all trying to light diyas at an open window. Dhruv laughed and showed them how to shield the flame.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv stuck at the bus shelter?
qa.a: His tram had been cancelled in the heavy rain.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he thought of Jaipur?
qa.a: A strong homesickness; he missed the noise, the rooftops and his cousins so much it felt like hunger.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv build belonging instead of going home?
qa.a: He kept his plan with Manoj and walked there, bringing his own festival to share with the new people he met.

qa.q: What might the evening be like for the Dutch colleagues and the neighbour?
qa.a: It was probably new and fun for them, and Dhruv showing them how to shield the flame let them join in rather than just watch 🎉

grounding: Shows a young migrant feeling nostalgia abroad yet keeping his festival and sharing it to build belonging in the new place.

passage:
Jagdish had lived in the Pune housing society for three months before anyone knew his name. In Kolkata, his whole para knew what he ate for breakfast.
He kept the things he couldn't give up: Sunday fish curry, even though rohu at the local market was expensive; Bengali songs while he ironed his shirts. But he'd stopped greeting people in the lift, embarrassed by his slow Marathi.
One evening Preeti from the fourth floor knocked because his music was coming through the wall. He apologised at once. She shook her head. "No, no. My mother used to sing this one. Can you send me the name?"
The next week she invited him to the society's Ganpati cleaning crew. He went, got paint on his only good kurta, and learnt the Marathi word for broom.
He still called his mother every Sunday at lunch. Now he had things to tell her.

qa.q: Why did Preeti knock on Jagdish's door?
qa.a: His music was coming through the wall.

qa.q: Why had Jagdish stopped greeting people in the lift?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his slow Marathi.

qa.q: What could Jagdish keep doing to belong while staying himself?
qa.a: He could keep his Sunday fish curry and Bengali songs while saying yes to invitations like the cleaning crew and practising Marathi bit by bit.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish's mother when he calls now?
qa.a: She probably hears a happier son with new stories, which may ease any worry about him being alone in Pune.

grounding: Shows a young man in a new city holding on to his food, music and language while slowly finding belonging with neighbours.
